definition: Model risk is the risk that the methodology or assumptions behind a valuation, pricing, or risk model are no longer valid — so the model's outputs stop reflecting reality — whether because the model contains fundamental errors or because a sound model is used incorrectly or outside the context it was designed for.
core_idea: Valuation, pricing, and risk models can quietly stop matching reality — through flawed construction, bad inputs, drifted assumptions, or misuse outside their intended scope — and organizations need deliberate re-validation, documentation, and independent risk controls (like position limits) to catch this before it causes losses.
key_points: Poor assumptions and badly designed models cause risk-management problems across all financial markets, but are especially common in energy given model complexity and the long periods models and assets remain in use.
Bad assumptions, poor parameter estimates, or flawed market data can lead to major financial losses.
A model can be adequate when built and still fail well before the asset's life ends, as regulations, population, or technology shift the underlying assumptions.
Employee turnover compounds the problem — original model developers are often gone before issues surface.
Organizations need a deliberate process to ensure someone still understands each model in production after years of use.
The main U.S. regulatory reference for model risk is the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance to banks, which is treated as broadly applicable to energy market models too.

The Federal Reserve traces model risk to two root causes: the model itself may contain fundamental errors, or a fundamentally sound model may be used incorrectly or outside the context it was designed for.
Fundamental errors can enter at any stage of building a model: choice of theory, sample design, numerical methods, selection of inputs, or system implementation.
Shortcuts or approximations adopted to make a hard problem tractable can quietly undermine the reliability of a model's outputs.
Output quality is bounded by the quality of input data and assumptions — bad inputs or wrong assumptions produce inaccurate outputs regardless of how well the model itself is built.
Misuse can be deliberate, such as applying an existing model to a new product or market, or unintentional, such as market conditions or customer behavior drifting away from what the model assumes.

Decision-makers need to understand a model's limitations — both its inherent shortcomings/approximations and the restricted scope its assumptions imply — to avoid using it inconsistently with its original intent.
There is an inherent trade-off between how simple a model is (and thus how easily it can be understood and checked) versus how completely it captures the real-world factors that drive outcomes.
All models are simplified versions of reality; something important can be left out, or something unnecessary can be included.
Simple models benefit from being checkable by a wide range of people, which is itself a guard against model risk.

Complex models incorporate more factors but are harder to understand, so it is unrealistic to expect people to verify parts of a model they don't understand, and it is often unclear exactly when such a model stops working correctly.
No model can be completely trusted, so risk controls should assume any given model could eventually be shown to be wrong.

Position limits cap a trading desk's exposure to bound the damage any single flawed model can cause, enforcing diversification across trading types rather than concentrating risk on one model's output.
The goal of position limits is bounding worst-case loss from a single point of model failure, not improving the model's accuracy.
relationships: Distinct risk category alongside VAR and counterparty/credit risk.
Sits under general risk management; grounded in Federal Reserve SR 11-7 guidance.
The complexity/checkability trade-off connects to why fundamental design errors happen and why documentation and appropriate-use practices matter as mitigations.
Position limits complement modeling reserves as a second, independent layer of model-risk control.
trading_implications: Long-lived asset valuations (power plants, pipelines, wells) should be periodically re-validated rather than trusted indefinitely once built.
Traders who rely on a model's pricing, valuation, or risk output can be exposed to losses if the model breaks quietly without anyone noticing.
A model built for one market or product can generate misleading trading signals if reused elsewhere without re-validating its assumptions.
Firms should weigh the benefit of added model sophistication against a reduced ability of staff to independently verify or catch failures.
A desk should not size positions purely off one model's confidence, since position limits exist precisely because that confidence could be misplaced.
caveats: SR 11-7 is Federal Reserve guidance written for banks; its application to energy market models is the author's extension, not a dedicated energy-market regulation.

Model risk cannot be fully eliminated by better model design alone — even a well-built model degrades if assumptions drift or it is used outside its intended context, which is why independent controls like position limits and reserves matter alongside model validation.
